title: Predictive Modeling of Residential Property Prices in Pierce County
text:
Preface
This documentation presents the project proposal and development progress for the Predictive Modeling of Residential Property Prices in Pierce County, developed as part of the Solution Engineering course at FHTW.
The project aims to build a robust machine learning pipeline to estimate housing prices by integrating diverse data sources from the Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer. This book serves as the central repository for project objectives, data descriptions, organizational structure, and development plans.

title: 1  Project Objective
text:
1.1 Background & Motivation
Estimating house prices is a classic regression problem with clear real-world importance. Housing markets are influenced by many interconnected factors, including property characteristics, location, neighborhood effects, and market trends over time. Because nearby properties often share similar values and market conditions change continuously, house-price prediction provides an excellent example for applying the complete data-science workflow covered in this course.
For this project, the publicly available Assessor–Treasurer data from Pierce County is used as the main data source. The dataset contains detailed and realistic information about properties, transactions, and assessments across multiple linked tables, offering a large-scale and practical environment for data exploration, pre-processing, feature engineering, and predictive modeling.

title: 1  Project Objective
text:
1.2 Project Goal
Develop a machine learning system capable of predicting residential property prices using structural, spatial, economic, and neighborhood characteristics.

Qualitative Objectives

Build a clean housing dataset for Pierce County.
Explore which factors influence house prices.
Engineer predictive variables from property and spatial data.
Compare traditional statistical and machine learning approaches.
Deploy a simple Shiny app for interactive price estimation.
Allow non-technical users to test predictions using custom property inputs.
Create visual outputs that support decision-making.

title: 2  Data Source Description & Data Dictionary
text:
2.1 Overview
The Pierce County Assessor–Treasurer Data Mart is a comprehensive relational database containing detailed property assessment, taxation, appraisal, land-use, improvement, and sales transaction records maintained by Pierce County, Washington. The dataset integrates information from multiple administrative systems and organizes it into interconnected tables linked primarily through the parcel identification number, enabling consistent tracking of individual properties across taxation, valuation, ownership, and structural characteristics.
The database includes information related to property accounts, land attributes, building improvements, tax assessments, exemption categories, sales history, and geographic identifiers. Together, these tables provide a multidimensional representation of residential and commercial properties and support both fiscal administration and real-estate market analysis.
Here we provide a data dictionary with detailed descriptions of the available tables, attributes, data types, and relationships that form the foundation for exploratory data analysis, spatial analysis, and predictive modeling of residential property prices in Pierce County.

10
Represents boundaries for land subject to similar social, environmental, economic and governmental forces. Text
10

All Mobile/Manufactured homes located on land owned by the Mobile/Manufactured home owner are coded with the Neighborhood Extension 0. Exception - Mobile/Manufactured homes located within a park and owned by the park owner, will carry the same Neighborhood Extension as the park. Table 3.3: Identified project risks and corresponding mitigation strategies.









Risk
Mitigation




Large number of tables / complex joins
Build join pipeline incrementally; validate row counts at each step


Many missing values in building details
Imputation strategies (median/mode); sensitivity analysis on imputed variables


Data covers multiple property types (commercial, mobile homes)
Filter to Residential Improved sales only at ingestion


Temporal drift in prices (market cycles)
Include sale year/month as features; optionally restrict to recent years


Skewed Sale Price distribution
Log-transform target; evaluate models on both scales


Shiny App complexity
Start with minimal viable app; add features iteratively

title: 6  Variable selection and Data Cleaning
text:
6.1 Subset the Data
After all the data has been mapped put in a database we construct the final selection of variables used for modelling and clean this data.
After mapping the data out and looking at the variable description, we limit the potentially used features. These features should be ones, that a homeowner likely knows about their house.
crumbs: 6  Variable selection and Data Cleaning

title: 6  Variable selection and Data Cleaning
text:
Land and Location Attributes
Restrict the features to: - land square feet - waterfront type - view quality - electricity availability - water availability - street type - coordinates (longitude, latitude)



Table 6.1: Selected appraisal account features: land and location attributes



Code
df_1 <- dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT parcel_no, appraisal_account_type, buildings, land_net_squarefeet, waterfront_type, view_quality,
  utility_electric, utility_water, street_type, latitude, longitude
  FROM "APPRAISAL_ACCOUNT"
  WHERE appraisal_account_type = \'Residential\'
')






Property Characteristics
We get property specifics: - condition - number of stories - number of bedrooms - number of bathrooms - units - year built - year remodeled



Table 6.2: Selected improvement features: building characteristics and construction details



Code
df_2 <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT i.parcel_no, i.building_id, i.property_type, i.condition,
         b.stories, b.bedrooms, b.bathrooms, b.units, b.year_built, b.year_remodeled
  FROM \"IMPROVEMENT\" i
  LEFT JOIN \"IMPROVEMENT_BUILT_AS\" b
    ON i.parcel_no = b.parcel_no
    AND i.building_id = b.building_id
  WHERE i.property_type = 'Residential'
")






Property Valuation
We get the current property value:



Table 6.3: Market value from tax account table (target variable)



Code
df_3 <- dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT parcel_no, total_market_value_current_year
  FROM "TAX_ACCOUNT"
')






Data Integration
We join the data together from all three source subsets:



Table 6.4: Integrated dataset combining land, improvement, and valuation features



Code
df_all <- df_1 %>%
  left_join(df_2, by = "parcel_no") %>%
  left_join(df_3, by = "parcel_no")






Cleaning
We obtain the dataset with selected features. Now we go ahead to prepare the data for initial exploratory data analysis.


Code
df_all <- df_all %>% 
  select( -property_type)


We first select lands with buildings on it, as we are interested in residential home valuations.


Code
df_all <- df_all %>% 
  filter(buildings != 0)


Then we look at the missing values and treat them one-by-one.

Code
colSums(is.na(df_all))




Table 6.5: Initial assessment of missing values across all features



                      parcel_no          appraisal_account_type 
                              0                               0 
                      buildings             land_net_squarefeet 
                              0                               3 
                waterfront_type                    view_quality 
                         256540                          252509 
               utility_electric                   utility_water 
                              0                               0 
                    street_type                        latitude 
                              0                               5 
                      longitude                     building_id 
                              5                           29816 
                      condition                         stories 
                          29816                           29846 
                       bedrooms                       bathrooms 
                          29846                           29846 
                          units                      year_built 
                          29887                           29846 
                 year_remodeled total_market_value_current_year 
                          42869                               0 




We remove observations that have no bedroom or bathroom recorded as these would be one of the features easiest for the user to input and we want to use them. If they are missing it likely hints at a data recording issue or a building type that is not a classical residential home (which is out of scope for this project).


Code
df_all <- df_all %>% 
  filter(!is.na(bathrooms))


We also remove the 5 observations missing coordinates or square footage.


Code
df_all <- df_all %>% 
  filter(!is.na(latitude) & !is.na(longitude) & !is.na(land_net_squarefeet))


Waterfront type records River, Lake, Stream/Creek or Salt. We fill in missing values to represent no waterfront, as such category does not exist and missing specification likely represents that the property ahs no direct water connection.


Code
df_all <- df_all %>% 
  mutate(waterfront_type = replace_na(waterfront_type, "None"))
unique(df_all$waterfront_type)


[1] "WF Salt"         "None"            "WF Lake"         "WF Stream/Creek"
[5] "WF River"       


View quality currently has 9 categories that is slightly excessive, and more confusing for the potential user and increases model complexity.


Code
unique(df_all$view_quality)


 [1] NA              "View Lim"      "View Lim -"    "View Lim +"   
 [5] "View Avg +"    "View Avg"      "View Good"     "View Good +"  
 [9] "View V-Good"   "View V-Good +"


We collapse the categories into “limited”, “average”, “good”, “very good”. We replace NAs with uncategorized.


Code
df_all <- df_all %>%
  mutate(
    view_quality = replace_na(view_quality, "uncategorized"),

    view_quality = fct_collapse(view_quality,
      "limited"   = c("View Lim", "View Lim -", "View Lim +"),
      "average"   = c("View Avg", "View Avg +"),
      "good"      = c("View Good", "View Good +"),
      "very good" = c("View V-Good", "View V-Good +")
    )
  )
unique(df_all$view_quality)


[1] uncategorized limited       average       good          very good    
Levels: uncategorized average good limited very good


We order the view types.


Code
df_all$view_quality <- factor(df_all$view_quality, 
                               levels = c("uncategorized", "limited", "average", "good", "very good"),
                               ordered = TRUE)


For the year remodeled, we will proceed as no remodeling happened, if the year is not recorded.


Code
df_all <- df_all %>% 
  mutate(year_remodeled = replace_na(year_remodeled, 0))


Lastly, in the units feature we convert the few missing values to 1 unit after looking into the data manually, and also convert 0 units to 1 as the empirical meaning of having no separate units and the whole unit being one (for example family home) is the same.


Code
df_all <- df_all %>%
  mutate(units = if_else(is.na(units) | units == 0, 1, units))


We have now the complete dataset with the preselected features.

Code
colSums(is.na(df_all))




Table 6.6: Final verification of missing values after cleaning (all zeros indicate complete data)



                      parcel_no          appraisal_account_type 
                              0                               0 
                      buildings             land_net_squarefeet 
                              0                               0 
                waterfront_type                    view_quality 
                              0                               0 
               utility_electric                   utility_water 
                              0                               0 
                    street_type                        latitude 
                              0                               0 
                      longitude                     building_id 
                              0                               0 
                      condition                         stories 
                              0                               0 
                       bedrooms                       bathrooms 
                              0                               0 
                          units                      year_built 
                              0                               0 
                 year_remodeled total_market_value_current_year 
                              0                               0 






Data Quality Validation
A few post checks we should still apply.


Code
unique(df_all$utility_electric)


[1] "POWER INSTALLED"    "POWER AVAILABLE"    "POWER NO - COMMENT"


Code
df_all <- df_all %>%
  mutate(utility_electric = str_replace(utility_electric, "POWER NO - COMMENT", "POWER NO"))
unique(df_all$utility_electric)


[1] "POWER INSTALLED" "POWER AVAILABLE" "POWER NO"       




Code
unique(df_all$utility_water)


[1] "WATER INSTALLED" "WATER NO"        "WATER AVAILABLE"




Code
unique(df_all$street_type)


[1] "STREET UNPAVED" "PAVED"          "STREET NO ROAD"


Check coordinate range.

Code
df_all %>%
  summarise(
    min_lat = min(latitude, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_lat = max(latitude, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_lon = min(longitude, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_lon = max(longitude, na.rm = TRUE)
  )




Table 6.7: Geographic bounding box of properties in the dataset



   min_lat  max_lat   min_lon   max_lon
1 46.73973 47.40335 -122.8406 -121.4681






Code
unique(df_all$condition)


[1] "Average"       "Extra Poor"    "Uninhabitable" "Poor"         
[5] "Fair"          "Very Poor"    


Code
df_all$condition <- factor(df_all$condition, 
                                levels = c("Uninhabitable", 
                                           "Extra Poor", 
                                           "Very Poor", 
                                           "Poor", 
                                           "Fair", 
                                           "Average"),
                                ordered = TRUE)




Code
df_all %>%
  select(stories, bedrooms, bathrooms) %>%  
  slice_max(order_by = stories, n = 5)


  stories bedrooms bathrooms
1      15        3      2.00
2      10        3      2.00
3       8        0      0.50
4       4        3      3.75
5       4        3      4.00


The top 3 observation are very unlikely with this combination of bedrooms and bathrooms, so we remove them.


Code
to_remove <- df_all %>%
  slice_max(order_by = stories, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE)

df_all <- df_all %>%
  anti_join(to_remove)


Joining with `by = join_by(parcel_no, appraisal_account_type, buildings,
land_net_squarefeet, waterfront_type, view_quality, utility_electric,
utility_water, street_type, latitude, longitude, building_id, condition,
stories, bedrooms, bathrooms, units, year_built, year_remodeled,
total_market_value_current_year)`


Looking at the data again manually, and in particular the combination of bathrooms and bedrooms with teh units we also detect some anomalies that we remove.


Code
df_all <- df_all %>%
  filter(bathrooms <= 17 & bedrooms <= 21)


The year remodeled being 0 means no remodeling has been recorded on the house.

Code
df_all %>%
  summarise(
    min_built     = min(year_built, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_built     = max(year_built, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_remodeled = min(year_remodeled, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_remodeled = max(year_remodeled, na.rm = TRUE)
  )




Table 6.8: Range of construction and renovation years (0 = no remodeling recorded)



  min_built max_built min_remodeled max_remodeled
1      1861      2026             0          2026




We additionally check if the year remodeled is not 0 it is always more recent than the year built.


Code
impossible_dates <- df_all %>%
  filter(year_remodeled > 0 & year_remodeled < year_built)

nrow(impossible_dates)


[1] 0


Check the valuation range.

Code
df_all %>%
  summarise(
    min_value     = min(total_market_value_current_year, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_value     = max(total_market_value_current_year, na.rm = TRUE)
  )




Table 6.9: Property valuation range in current year market values (in USD)



  min_value max_value
1      8400  10627600






Code
#save(df_all, file = here::here("data", "df_all.RData"))
